source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: With the same dialogue context, LLM turns contain far fewer grounding acts (clarification, follow-up, acknowledgment) than human experts. LLMs presume common ground instead of building it.
numbers: Off-the-shelf LLM generations are 77.5% less likely to contain grounding acts than humans. Follow-ups average 64.3% fewer, acknowledgments 83.4% fewer. Datasets: ESConv, Persuasion for Good, TSCC.
quote: LLMs generate language with less conversational grounding than humans
limits: Simulated turn-taking, not live users. Grounding acts detected by few-shot LLM classifiers checked against humans (kappa about 0.7 to 0.8).
agent_relevance: A default LLM agent will not ask what do you mean. If common ground matters, the scaffold must force a check step.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: Agreement with humans on WHERE grounding acts occur is poor. Instruction tuning (SFT) does not help; preference optimisation hurts.
numbers: Cohen kappa mostly below 0.3 for ChatGPT-3.5 vs humans. SFT checkpoints: Pearson correlation about 0, p>0.1. PPO: base rate falls 7.0% and kappa 39.0% on average. DPO: base rate falls 12.1%, kappa 42.5% (Archangel models, Mistral 7B).
limits: Small open models; only ESConv ablations in depth; preference data are synthetic (UltraFeedback).
agent_relevance: RLHF-style preference training pushes models toward presumptive answers. Do not assume a helpful-tuned model grounds.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: Preference data penalise grounding: questions are rarer in preferred answers than in dispreferred ones. A prompt fix over-corrects.
numbers: Questions appear in 11.83% of UltraChat samples; in 13.77% of preferred vs 18.35% of dispreferred UltraFeedback answers. Prompt mitigation on ChatGPT-3.5: follow-ups 10.76% to 42.32%, acknowledgment 1.05% to 2.54%, clarification 0 to 1.16%, but agreement with humans stays low (overeager grounding).
limits: Single model for the prompt test.
agent_relevance: Asking more is not asking at the right place. Trigger clarification by a code-checked condition, not by a blanket instruction.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Failure taxonomy of 14 modes in 3 groups, built from 150 traces and scaled to 1600+ annotated traces over several multi-agent frameworks. Several modes are common-ground failures (ignored input, withheld information, no clarification, reasoning-action mismatch).
numbers: Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source MAS. Human annotator kappa 0.88; LLM annotator accuracy 94%, kappa 0.77. Mode shares in the first 150-trace analysis: proceeding with wrong assumptions instead of asking clarification 6.8%, ignoring other agent's input 1.9%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, incomplete verification 8.2%, incorrect verification 9.1%.
limits: Shares differ between the first analysis and the later 1600-trace table. Mostly GPT-4o-class backbones; open-source frameworks.
agent_relevance: Coordination failure in agent teams is mostly specification, misalignment and verification, not raw capability.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Targeted fixes help only modestly. Clearer role specification alone raised ChatDev success.
numbers: +9.4% task success for ChatDev (GPT-4o) from improved role specification with the same user prompt. Authors say robust reliability needs structural, not only prompt, fixes.
limits: Case-study intervention, one framework.
agent_relevance: Shared role and task specs matter, but are not enough. Code-level verification is still needed.

source: Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone (2024) When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Human-AI teams on average do worse than the best of human alone or AI alone.
numbers: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes (studies Jan 2020 to June 2023). Hedges g = -0.23, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.07.
limits: Possible publication bias; heterogeneous designs; mostly pre-LLM-agent systems.
agent_relevance: Pairing does not automatically add up. Joint activity needs designed coordination, not just presence.

source: Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone (2024) When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Task type moderates: decision tasks lose, creation tasks tend to gain.
numbers: Decision tasks g = -0.27 (95% CI -0.44 to -0.10, p=0.002). Creation tasks g = +0.19 (CI -0.09 to 0.48, p=0.18, n=34). Difference significant, F(1,104)=7.84, p=0.006.
limits: Creation gain not significantly above zero on its own.
agent_relevance: Use a second agent or human for open generation, not for closed-choice verdicts.

source: Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone (2024) When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Relative skill moderates: when humans beat AI alone, the combination gains; when AI beats humans, the combination loses.
numbers: Data type also moderates synergy, F(4,101)=15.24, p<0.001. Relative-performance moderator significant for synergy and augmentation.
limits: Observational moderators, not randomised.
agent_relevance: Defer to the stronger partner on a given sub-task; do not average.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When a task is spread over turns (shared understanding must build up), every tested LLM does much worse than when fully specified in one turn.
numbers: Average drop 39% across 6 generation tasks, 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude loss about 15%, unreliability up 112%. Top models fall from 90%+ in the single-turn lab setting.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated user with sharded instructions; default temperature 1.
agent_relevance: Models make early assumptions and over-rely on them. Re-state and re-check shared state rather than trusting turn history.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Mechanism: early wrong assumptions, premature full answers, over-reliance on own earlier answer, bloated later answers. A control that gives all information at once (CONCAT) shows the loss comes from the conversation, not from sharding the text.
numbers: Four behaviours named by the authors; CONCAT degradation is larger for smaller models.
limits: Exact CONCAT averages not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Supports a restate-then-solve step: collapse the conversation into one consolidated spec before answering.

source: Wu et al. (2025) CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
finding: Training with multi-turn-aware rewards (simulate future turns with a user) makes models ask and clarify, improving collaboration.
numbers: Vs baselines: +18.5% task performance, +13.3% more efficient conversations, +46.3% interactivity (LLM judge). User study with 201 judges: satisfaction +17.6%, user time -10.4%. The model asks questions about 50% of the time.
limits: Gains come from RL fine-tuning, not a scaffold. Simulated users in training; three task domains.
agent_relevance: Shows the grounding gap in b02 is fixable by long-horizon reward. A scaffold can only imitate this with explicit clarify steps.

source: Li et al. (2023) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: In a 3-agent text game, LLM teams coordinate and show some first and second-order ToM, but fail through long-horizon context loss and hallucinated task state. An explicit belief state helps.
numbers: ToM inference accuracy: ChatGPT 41.9% (1st-order) and 11.6% (2nd-order); GPT-4 60.0% and 64.3%; GPT-4 + explicit belief state 80.1% and 69.4%. Introspection 79.0%, 80.0%, 97.2%. Rounds to finish: GPT-4 12.3, GPT-4+belief 11.0.
limits: One text-game environment, few trials per condition; baselines MAPPO and a planner.
agent_relevance: An explicit, program-held shared state beats relying on the model to remember. Matches our schema logic (code holds state).

source: Agashe et al. (2025) LLM-Coordination: Evaluating and Analyzing Multi-agent Coordination Abilities in LLMs
finding: LLM agents match or beat RL in coordination games solved from environment state (Overcooked), but struggle where partner beliefs matter (Hanabi). In CoordQA, ToM and joint planning are weak.
numbers: CoordQA: 198 multiple-choice questions over 3 abilities. Environment comprehension best, ToM worse, joint planning worst (some models below random). LLM agents adapt to unseen partners, unlike self-play RL.
limits: Headline claims from abstract and intro; per-model numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Common ground that depends on modelling a partner's beliefs is the weak spot.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Failed robustness replication: trivial changes to false-belief tasks (for example a transparent bag) keep the model giving the original, now wrong, answer. The earlier success was brittle.
numbers: Original prompt: P(chocolate)=99% for the belief about a mislabelled bag. Transparent-bag variant: model still gives about 95 to 98% chocolate for a person who can see inside.
quote: the zero-hypothesis for model evaluation in intuitive psychology should be skeptical
limits: Small hand-built variant set; GPT-3.5-era models; later models improved.
agent_relevance: Treat model ToM skeptically and judge by worst case. Do not let the agent rely on claimed mind-reading.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
finding: In conversations with information asymmetry, models can answer the belief question but fail the prerequisite questions about who knows what. Illusory ToM.
numbers: Human All-question-types score 87.5% (graduate students, 32 sets); human 90.6% on answerability and info-access lists. All LLMs far lower; Mistral Instruct + CoT 0.1% on All. Chain-of-thought helps but a large gap stays; fine-tuned Flan-T5 XL still short of humans.
quote: some instances of successful LLM ToM reasoning in FANToM should be interpreted as illusory
limits: Human baseline small. Per-model figure values read from a garbled chart.
agent_relevance: Test consistency across question types before trusting a shared-knowledge claim.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Whether coordination across agents helps depends on task structure and the single-agent baseline.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures, 3 LLM families. Relative change vs single agent from +80.8% (decomposable finance) to -70.0% (sequential planning). Capability ceiling: tasks above about 45% single-agent accuracy get negative returns from more agents (beta=-0.236, p=0.004). Cross-validated R2=0.373.
limits: Predictive fit is modest.
agent_relevance: Coordination has a cost. Use it only for decomposable work and when the baseline is weak.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Centralised verification contains error propagation; independent agents amplify it.
numbers: Independent systems amplify trace-level errors 17.2x; centralised coordination 4.4x. Tool-heavy tasks (16 tools) suffer multi-agent overhead. Best architecture predicted for 87% of held-out configurations.
limits: Same study.
agent_relevance: A single checker that sees all outputs is the cheap way to keep a team's shared picture correct.

source: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate -- We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity (2025)
finding: Failed claim: multi-agent debate often does not beat Chain-of-Thought or self-consistency, even with more compute. Model heterogeneity helps.
numbers: 5 MAD methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 foundation models; MAD generally fails to outperform CoT and Self-Consistency.
limits: Only abstract and framing read; no per-benchmark numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Do not build a debate team as a default. Same-model agents share blind spots.

source: Cross et al. (2025) Hypothetical Minds: Scaffolding Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Tasks with LLMs
finding: A scaffold that generates, tests and revises natural-language hypotheses about another agent's strategy beats LLM and RL baselines in Melting Pot. Hypothesis evaluation and refinement are the key parts (ablations).
numbers: Domains: competitive, mixed-motive, collaborative, dyadic and population-based. No numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract level only; Melting Pot agents, not human teaming.
agent_relevance: A partner model kept as a testable hypothesis, scored against observed behaviour, is a usable scaffold operator.

source: Keysar, Barr, Balin, Brauner (2000) Taking perspective in conversation: the role of mutual knowledge in comprehension
finding: Adult addressees consider referents the director cannot see. Common ground is used late, as a correction, not at the start.
numbers: Exp 1 (about 21 participants): in 23% of test trials the hand reached for the hidden object (6% corrected, 17% moved it). Shared referent fixation delayed 503 ms; trial time 242 ms longer in test condition. Exp 2: 20% reached (5%) or grabbed (15%); first fixation on target delayed 1,045 ms in one measure and 1,783 ms in another.
limits: Confederate director with scripted instructions; small samples; objects hidden in slots.
agent_relevance: Egocentric first, perspective second. An agent that holds all the context may read ambiguous instructions through its own context.

source: Santiesteban, Shah, White, Bird, Heyes (2015) Mentalizing or submentalizing in a communication task?
finding: Rival explanation for the director task: errors reflect object-centred spatial coding, not perspective-taking. A camera works as well as a human director, and people with autism are not impaired.
numbers: Accuracy director condition M=.79 (SEM .03) vs camera condition M=.80 (SEM .03); condition effect F(1.01,36.51)=0.034, p=.86; group effect F(1,36)<1. N about 38 (ASD and controls).
limits: Small N; null result; the submentalizing account is itself disputed.
agent_relevance: Late use of common ground may not need mind-reading at all. Weakens the claim that humans model partner knowledge by default.

source: Samuel, Roehr-Brackin, Jelbert, Clayton (2019) Flexible egocentricity: asymmetric switch costs on a perspective-taking task
finding: Moderator: people are egocentric by default, but the bias goes away briefly after they adopt another perspective. Returning to one's own view costs time; moving to the other view does not.
numbers: 40 participants. Faster to select from the informed (shared-view) director than the ignorant director; slowed by a visible inactive second director; significant switch cost only when returning to own perspective.
limits: Computerised avatars; one lab; 40 participants.
agent_relevance: Taking the partner's view first may cheapen later checks. Suggests putting the partner-view restatement first.

source: DeChurch and Mesmer-Magnus (2010) The cognitive underpinnings of effective teamwork: a meta-analysis (Journal of Applied Psychology)
finding: Team cognition (shared mental models, transactive memory) predicts team process, motivation and performance, and adds prediction beyond behaviour and motivation.
numbers: 231 correlations from 65 studies (from a search summary of the abstract; not read in full).
limits: Not opened beyond abstract; effect sizes taken from the 2017 update line.
agent_relevance: Background support that shared understanding raises team performance.

source: Mesmer-Magnus, Niler, Plummer, Larson, DeChurch (2017) The cognitive underpinnings of effective teamwork: a continuation
finding: Replication on an updated, nearly doubled database: team cognition still predicts process and performance.
numbers: 128 independent studies (about twice the 65 in 2010). Team cognition and performance: k=107, n=7,775 teams, r=.30, corrected rho=.35, 95% CI .31 to .39, 80% credibility .16 to .55. With team behavioural process: k=44, n=2,973, r=.32, rho=.38.
limits: Correlational; wide credibility intervals mean moderators matter; human teams.
agent_relevance: Shared understanding is worth about r=.3 on performance in human teams. A realistic size for any agent scaffold effect.

source: Mesmer-Magnus et al. (2017) The cognitive underpinnings of effective teamwork: a continuation (moderators)
finding: Moderator: nature of emergence. Similar knowledge across members (compositional) is stronger for performance; complementary knowledge (compilational) is stronger for process.
numbers: Performance: compositional k=55, n=4,678, rho=.39; compilational k=62, n=3,766, rho=.29. Process: compositional rho=.32 (k=31); compilational rho=.44 (k=14, wide CI .02 to .86).
limits: Ordering reverses across outcomes; heterogeneous; small k for process.
agent_relevance: Overlap of knowledge helps performance. Our roles need both a shared brief and distinct roles.

source: DeChurch and Mesmer-Magnus (2010) Measuring Shared Team Mental Models: A Meta-Analysis (Group Dynamics)
finding: Measurement method moderates the shared-mental-model effect. Structure-capturing methods predict process; questionnaires do not.
numbers: SMM and team process: k=17, N=1,238, r=.20. SMM and team performance: k=19, N=1,363, r=.29. Process by method: similarity ratings r=.24 (k=6), questionnaire r=.04 (k=5). Performance by method: similarity r=.20 (k=9), concept mapping r=.28 (k=6), questionnaire r=.32 (k=6, high spread).
limits: Small k per cell; table values read from PDF layout.
agent_relevance: How shared understanding is measured changes the conclusion. A code-checked comparison of two restatements is more trustworthy than self-report.
